Theme

School & learning · Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas

experiment noun and verb

also experiments, scientific experiment, test, trial, try out, experiment with, experimental

classical

Quint. 2.5.15: minus valent praecepta quam experīmenta
Plin. NH 29.18, of doctors: discunt perīculīs nostrīs et experīmenta per mortēs agunt
M-O s.v. experiment (Trappen 1843)

experīmentum, experīmentī n.

noun, second declension · Declension on Wiktionary

a trial, a test; an experiment; experience

A proof, test or trial, and so what is learnt by it, experience (Lewis & Short: once in Cicero, Tusc. 3.74, common after Augustus). The scientists kept it for an experiment (Morgan–Owens). To make one: experīmentum facere, or with Prudentius experīmentum capere, to put to the test.

Other words

  • perīculum facere — to make trial of, test, try out

    also used · classical · Ter. Eun. 475–476; Cic. Verr. 1.34: alicujus fideī perīculum facere (Lewis & Short)

    The older idiom, with the genitive of what is tried. Perīculum is first a trial; its common sense is the risk that goes with one, danger, so the phrase needs its genitive or its context to be heard as a test.

  • experior, experīrī, expertus sum — try, test, put to the proof; experience

    verb, fourth conjugation, deponent · also used · classical · Cic. Cael. 58: vim ejus esse expertum in servō (Lewis & Short) · Conjugation on Wiktionary

    The verb for “to experiment”: to try a thing out, and to learn by trying.

Examples

  • Crēscit audācia experīmentō.

    Their courage grows as they try it.Plin. Ep. 9.33.6

  • fac periclum in litterīs, fac in palaestrā, in mūsicīs

    try him out in letters, in the wrestling-school, in musicTer. Eun. 475–476

  • coctum est, dēvorā, et experīmentum cape sit crūdum an assum suāvius

    it’s cooked: eat it up, and find out whether raw or roast tastes betterPrud. Perist. 2.406–408

See also try, test condition, research, science, prove.
